clue.text: Occasioned no gentleman being out of employment

indicators.note: the cad is being outside the word for employment, wrapping round it

parts.note: a cad is a man who behaves dishonourably, the opposite of a gentleman
use means employment, as in 'put to use'

explanation.surface: A man of low character was the cause of someone losing their job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being out of' reads as unemployment in the surface, but it tells you the cad stands outside the word for employment.
explanation.definitionFit: To occasion something is to bring it about, a synonym of produced or brought on.

clue.text: Short, short, long — the sound of Anna on the ski trail

indicators.note: the following words are spoken and heard as another word

parts.note: a piste is a ski run, so Anna on it is Anna-piste

explanation.surface: Describing the pattern of Anna's swishes as she skis down the slope.
explanation.definitionFit: This metrical foot has two unstressed syllables followed by a stressed one.
Shadowed means darkened; to shadow someone is to follow them closely, as a dog does.

parts.note: Sherlock's brother is Mycroft, but here a T has become F; a sleuth's name with a faulty letter fits a sleuth word with one letter swapped the same way

explanation.walkthrough: The page prints Mycroff, deliberately: put F for T in a word for a sleuth and you get a word meaning faulty.
explanation.definitionFit: Faulty or flawed; the misspelt name has one letter wrong, just as the word is a sleuth word with an F.

clue.text: How Judge Jeffreys dealt with twelve indecisive men?

definitions.text: How Judge Jeffreys dealt with twelve indecisive men?

parts.words: How Judge Jeffreys dealt with twelve indecisive men?
parts.note: Jeffreys was the notorious 'hanging judge'; twelve men who cannot agree are a deadlocked jury, which he would string up

explanation.walkthrough: Judge Jeffreys was a 17th-century English judge famous for the many executions after the Monmouth rebellion.
explanation.definitionFit: A jury of twelve unable to reach a verdict is the standard legal term for a deadlocked panel.

indicators.note: the letters of the composer's name and the words that follow are changed into a new order

explanation.surface: Franz Lehar finishes a muddle and rewrites an opera.
explanation.walkthrough: Lehar was the Hungarian composer of 'The Merry Widow', so the surface is about operetta; the answer is Humperdinck's opera.
explanation.definitionFit: Humperdinck's 1893 opera is based on the Grimm fairy tale of two children in the forest.

clue.text: Old boys readily spout to willing listeners

indicators.note: what is heard by those listening is a sound-alike, not the spelling

parts.note: hot springs that readily spout water are geysers

explanation.surface: Elderly men are always happy to talk to anyone who will listen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Marsh.' in the held text is stray print from the next column. 'Geezer' is British slang for a man, especially an old one.
explanation.definitionFit: Geezer is informal British slang for a man, often an elderly one.

clue.text: Small-scale — not, like the style of Pope's Homer

parts.note: un- is the prefix meaning not

parts.words: like the style of Pope's Homer
parts.note: Alexander Pope translated Homer into heroic couplets, the heroic style

explanation.surface: Pope's translation of Homer was a grand epic, not a modest work.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacking grandeur or epic quality, so modest and on a minor scale.

clue.text: Time of year when you'll get knotted, say?

indicators.note: the words are spoken and heard as a different word

parts.note: you'll be tied, as with a knot

explanation.surface: A season when people get married, tying the knot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'WANTED.' in the held text is stray print. 'Get knotted' also suggests getting drunk or being told to go away.
explanation.definitionFit: Yuletide is the Christmas season, a period in the calendar.

clue.text: Short passage recalls the smell-of midnight oil?

parts.note: para is the short form of paragraph, a passage of text

indicators.note: calls back, so the word for the smell is read in reverse

parts.note: niff is British slang for a bad smell

explanation.surface: A brief bit of writing brings back the scent of late-night study.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recalls' turns NIFF into FFIN. 'Burning the midnight oil' means working late, traditionally by an oil lamp.
explanation.definitionFit: Lamps for late-night working burned kerosene, the fuel the British call by this name.

clue.text: False god around the service station

indicators.note: the false god's name goes around the word 'the', enclosing it

parts.note: Bel is a Babylonian deity, a false god in the Bible
taken as written

explanation.surface: An idol has been set up around a motorway filling station.
explanation.walkthrough: 'service station' looks like a garage, but it means a place where religious services are held.
explanation.definitionFit: A Bethel is a nonconformist chapel, a building for church services.

indicators.note: the cry goes inside the word for unprotected

parts.note: bare means exposed or unprotected
ouch is the cry of someone in pain

explanation.surface: Someone yells in pain while riding in an open coach.
explanation.definitionFit: A barouche is a four-wheeled horse-drawn carriage with a collapsible hood.

explanation.surface: Someone searches for a small wild animal.
explanation.definitionFit: To ferret about is to search busily; the animal is a domesticated form of the polecat.

parts.note: words of praise carved where all can read them, for someone who can never say thank you because they are dead

explanation.definitionFit: Inscriptions on gravestones honour the dead, who cannot respond to praise.

indicators.note: squiffy means tipsy, so the words stagger into a new order

explanation.surface: Servants enjoy their gin and become drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: Hirelings are people employed for menial work, labourers paid by the job.
To stud is to dot or scatter over a surface; a collar stud fastens a detachable collar at the neck.

clue.text: Stone to press forward to get fish

parts.note: st is the abbreviation for stone, the British unit of weight
to urge on is to press forward or drive ahead

explanation.surface: Weight training pushing someone forward to land a catch.
explanation.definitionFit: A large bony-plated fish whose roe is caviar.

clue.text: Wave goes back-helped on its way?

explanation.definitionFit: An undertow is the current pulling back beneath breaking waves; something under tow is being pulled along.

clue.text: Heart trouble ending in death? Hamlet wondered

definitions.text: Heart trouble ending in death? Hamlet wondered

parts.words: Heart trouble ending in death? Hamlet wondered
parts.note: the word wanted is the ending of that heart trouble

explanation.walkthrough: Hamlet's soliloquy says 'by a sleep to say we end the heart-ache'; the answer is the last part of that compound.
explanation.definitionFit: A pain or soreness, here the second half of the word Shakespeare used for grief.

clue.text: Head broken and torn needs a sticker

indicators.note: the word head is broken and its letters rearranged

parts.note: rent is the past tense of rend, so torn

explanation.surface: A broken head and torn skin need a sticking plaster.
explanation.definitionFit: A follower who sticks to a cause or leader, a supporter.

clue.text: Blossom takes beer, maybe, in college dining-room

indicators.note: the dining room takes in the other letters, holding them inside

parts.note: hall is the dining room of a college at Oxford or Cambridge

indicators.note: the word beer may be arranged otherwise, so its letters are mixed

explanation.surface: A girl named Blossom has a drink in the college refectory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blossom' looks like a girl's name in the surface; it is the definition, a wild flower. 'maybe' scrambles the beer before the hall takes it in.
explanation.definitionFit: A harebell is a wild flower with blue bell-shaped flowers.
Rendering is coating a wall with plaster; to render a piece of music is to perform it.

parts.note: not an actor's return to the profession but simply walking onto the stage again

explanation.definitionFit: An actor who goes back on to the boards during a play comes in a second time.
To reek can mean to give off smoke or vapour, and also to stink.

indicators.note: the magistrates' title goes about the money, surrounding it

parts.note: reeves were local officials or magistrates in medieval England
L is the abbreviation for pound (libra)
the numeral one looks like the letter I

explanation.surface: A pound is enough to lift the load from some elderly justices.
explanation.walkthrough: In old print £1 was written with a capital L for libra and the figure 1, read here as the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: To relieve someone is to ease or lighten their load.
An estate is everything a dead person leaves; the three estates of the realm are social orders or classes.

clue.text: Offered to nurse a broken reed

parts.note: to nurse is to tend

indicators.note: the word reed is broken and its letters reassembled

explanation.surface: A carer gave help with a snapped stalk.
explanation.definitionFit: Tendered means put forward or proffered, as a resignation or payment is.

parts.note: not a costume drama but a film recording events as they happened, which later become history

explanation.definitionFit: A short cinema film of current events, shown before the main feature, becomes a record of history.
To settle a matter is to decide it; a bird settles when it lands or alights.
